trace.e: From Middle English trace, traas, from Old French trace (“an outline, track, trace”), from the verb (see below).

From Middle English tracen, from Old French tracer, trasser (“to delineate, score, trace", also, "to follow, pursue”), probably a conflation of Vulgar Latin *tractiō (“to delineate, score, trace”), from Latin trahere (“to draw”); and Old French traquer (“to chase, hunt, pursue”), from trac (“a track, trace”).

track.e: From Middle English trak, tracke, from Old French trac (“track of horses, trail, trace”), of uncertain origin. Likely from a Germanic source, either Old Norse traðk ("a track; path; trodden spot"; > Icelandic traðk (“a track; path; tread”), Faroese traðk (“track.
track.g: A mark left by something that has passed along.

trackless.e: From track (noun) + -less (suffix meaning ‘lacking or without something’).
trackless.g: Of a place: not having tracks or paths; pathless, untrodden; also, having had all tracks removed.

tract.e: From Middle English tract, tracte, traht (“a treatise, exposition, commentary”), from Old English traht, tract (“a treatise, exposition, commentary, text, passage”); and also from Middle English tract, tracte (“an expanse of space or time”); both from Latin tractus (“a haul, drawing, a drawing out”), the perfect passive participle of trahō.
From Latin tractus, the participle stem of trahere (“to pull, drag”).

trade.e: From Middle English trade (“path, course of conduct”), introduced into English by Hanseatic merchants, from Middle Low German trade (“track, course”), from Old Saxon trada (“spoor, track”), from Proto-West Germanic *tradu, from Proto-Germanic *tradō (“track, way”), and cognate with Old English tredan (“to tread”).
trade.g: The buying and selling of goods and services on a market.

tradition.e: From Middle English tradicioun, from Old French tradicion, from Latin trāditiō, from the verb trādō.
tradition.g: A part of culture that is passed from person to person or generation to generation, possibly differing in detail from family to family, such

traffick.e: Use of this spelling for the verb in relation to illegal trafficking is probably influenced by the spelling of the noun trafficking.
traffick.g: Alternative spelling of traffic (now especially of illegal goods)

tragedy.e: From the Middle English tragedie, from the Old French tragedie, from the Latin tragoedia, from the Ancient Greek τραγῳδία (tragōidía, “epic play, tragedy”).
tragedy.g: A drama or similar work, in which the main character is brought to ruin or otherwise suffers the extreme consequences of some tragic flaw or

trail.e: From Middle English trailen, from Old French trailler (“to tow; pick up the scent of a quarry”), from Vulgar Latin *tragulāre (“to drag”), from Latin tragula (“dragnet, javelin thrown by a strap”), probably related to Latin trahere (“to pull, drag along”).
trail.g: To follow behind (someone or something); to tail (someone or something).

train.e: From Middle English trayne (“train”), from Old French train (“a delay, a drawing out”), from traïner (“to pull out, to draw”), from Vulgar Latin *traginō, from *tragō, from Latin trahō (“to pull, to draw”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *tregʰ- (“to pull, draw, drag”).
From Middle English trayne (“treachery”), from Anglo-Norman traine, Middle French traïne, from traïr (“to betray”).

trait.e: Borrowed from Middle French trait (“line, feature”), from Latin tractus (“drawing, pulling”), from Latin trahō.
trait.g: An identifying characteristic, habit or trend.

traitor.e: From Middle English traitor, traitour, traytour, from Old French traïtor (French traître), from Latin trāditor. The general Old English word denoting "traitor" was lǣwa or lǣwend.
traitor.g: Someone who violates an allegiance and betrays their country; someone guilty of treason; one who, in breach of trust, delivers their country

traitorous.e: From Middle English trayterous, traytrous, (also Middle English traytours, treytours), from Anglo-Norman traiterous, traitourous and Old French traitros.

trample.e: From Middle English tramplen, trampelen (“to walk heavily”), equivalent to tramp + -le.
trample.g: To crush something by walking on it.

trance.e: From Middle English traunce, from Anglo-Norman transe (“fear of coming evil; passage from life to death”), from transir (“to be numb with fear; to die, pass on”), from Latin trānseō (“to cross over”).

tranquil.e: Borrowed from Middle French tranquille, from Latin tranquillus, from trāns- + the root of quiēs (“rest, quiet, peace”), ultimately from *kʷyeh₁- (“to rest”).
tranquil.g: Free from emotional or mental disturbance.

tranquillity.e: From tranquil + -ity, from Middle English tranquillite, from Old French tranquillite, tranquilité, from Latin tranquillitas.
tranquillity.g: The state of being tranquil; peacefulness, the absence of disturbance or stress; serenity; calm.

transfer.e: From Latin trānsferō (“to bear across”). Distant doublet of translate.
transfer.g: To move or pass from one place, person or thing to another.

transfigure.g: To transform the outward appearance of; to convert into a different form, state or substance.

transform.e: From Middle English transformen, from Old French transformer, from Latin transformo, transformare, from trans (“across”, preposition) + forma (“form”).
transform.g: To change greatly the appearance or form of.

transgress.e: From Middle English transgressen, from Old French transgresser and Latin transgressus, past participle of transgredior.
transgress.g: To exceed or overstep some limit or boundary.

transgression.e: From Middle English transgressioun, from Old French transgression, from Late Latin trānsgressiō, from Latin trānsgressus (perfect active participle of trānsgredior (“to step across”)) + -iō.
transgression.g: A violation of a law, duty or commandment.

transgressor.e: From Middle English transgressour, from Anglo-Norman transgressour, from Latin transgressor. Equivalent to transgress + -or.

translate.e: From Middle English translaten (“to transport, translate, transform”), from Anglo-Norman translater, from Latin trānslātus, perfect passive participle of trānsferō (“to transport, carry across, translate”). Distant doublet of transfer, see collate and confer, delate and defer, as well as prelate and prefer among others.
translate.g: Senses relating to the change of information, etc., from one form to another.

translation.e: From Middle English translacioun (“transfer, translation”), from Anglo-Norman translacioun, from Latin trānslātiō, from trānslāt-, the supine stem of trānsferō (“to transfer, transport, transform, translate”). Equivalent to translate + -ion.
translation.g: The act of translating, in its various senses:

transmit.e: From Middle English transmitten, borrowed from Latin trānsmittō (“transmit”, verb, literally “across-send”).
transmit.g: To send or convey from one person, place or thing to another.

transparent.e: Borrowed from Medieval Latin trānspārēns, trānspārēntis (“transparent”), present participle of transpareō, from Latin trans + pareō.
transparent.g: See-through, clear; having the property that light passes through it almost undisturbed, such that one can see through it clearly.

transplant.e: From Middle English transplaunten, from Old French transplanter, from Late Latin transplantare, equivalent to trans- + plant.
transplant.g: To uproot (a growing plant), and plant it in another place.

transport.e: From Middle English transporten, a borrowing from Old French transporter (“carry or convey across”), from Latin trānsportāre (“to carry over, take across, carry, convey, remove, transport”), from trāns- (“across, over, to the farther side of”) + portō (“to bear, carry, convey, take”).
transport.g: To carry or bear from one place to another; to remove; to convey.

transporting.e: From Middle English transportyng, equivalent to transport + -ing.

trap.e: From Middle English trappe, from Old English træppe, treppe (“trap, snare”) (also in betræppan (“to trap”)) from Proto-West Germanic *trappjā (“trap, snare”), from Proto-West Germanic *trappjan (“to step”), from Proto-Germanic *trapjaną (“to tread, stamp”), from Proto-Indo-European *drebʰ- (“to step, trip, trample”).
trap.g: A machine or other device designed to catch (and sometimes kill) animals, either by holding them in a container, or by catching hold of part

trap.e: Borrowed from Swedish trapp (“step, stair, stairway”), from Middle Low German trappe (“stair, step”).
trap.g: A dark coloured igneous rock; (now usually) any nongranitic igneous rock.

travail.e: From Middle English travail, borrowed from Old French travail (“suffering, torment”), deverbal from travailler, from Vulgar Latin *tripāliāre (“to torment”), from Latin tripālium (“torture device”) + -āre (verb-forming suffix).
travail.g: Arduous or painful exertion; excessive labor, suffering, hardship.

travail.e: From Middle English travailen, from Old French travailler, from the noun (see above).

travel.e: From Middle English travelen (“to make a laborious journey, travel”) from Middle Scots travailen (“to toil, work, travel”), alteration of Middle English travaillen (“to toil, work”), from Old French travailler (“to trouble, suffer, be worn out”).
travel.g: To be on a journey, often for pleasure or business and with luggage; to go from one place to another.

travel.e: From Middle English travail, travell, from Old French travail, travaille, travaillie, traval, travalle, traveaul, traveil, traveille, travel.
travel.g: The act of traveling; passage from place to place.

traveller.e: From Middle English traveler, travelour, travailere, travailour (“worker", also "traveller”), equivalent to travel + -er.
traveller.g: One who travels, especially to distant lands.

traverse.e: From Middle English traversen, from Old French traverser, from Latin trans (“across”) + versus (“turned”), perfect passive participle of Latin vertere (“to turn”).
traverse.g: A route used in mountaineering, specifically rock climbing, in which the descent occurs by a different route than the ascent.

tray.e: From Middle English trey, from Old English trēġ, trīġ (“wooden board, tray”), from Proto-West Germanic *trauwi, from Proto-Germanic *trawją (“wooden vessel”), from Proto-Indo-European *drewo-, *dóru (“tree; wood”).
tray.g: A small, typically rectangular or round, flat, and rigid object upon which things are carried.

tray.e: From Middle English traye, treie, from Old English trega (“misfortune, misery, trouble, grief, pain”), from Proto-Germanic *tregô (“mourning”), from Proto-Indo-European *dreǵʰ- (“unwilling, sullen, slack”).

treacherous.e: From Old French trecheros, tricheros (“deceitful”), equivalent to treacher + -ous.

treachery.e: From Middle English trecherie, from Old French tricherie, trecherie, from tricher, trichier (“to cheat”).
treachery.g: Deliberate, often calculated, disregard for trust or faith.

tread.e: From Middle English treden, from Old English tredan, from Proto-West Germanic *tredan, from Proto-Germanic *trudaną.
tread.g: To step or walk (on or across something); to trample.

tread.e: From Middle English tred, from treden (“to tread”).
tread.g: A step taken with the foot.

treader.e: From Middle English tredere, equivalent to tread + -er.

treading.e: From Middle English tredynge, tredyng; equivalent to tread + -ing.
treading.g: The act of one who treads.

treason.e: From Middle English tresoun, treison, from Anglo-Norman treson, from Old French traïson (“treason”), from trair, or from Latin trāditiō (“a giving up, handing over, surrender, delivery, tradition”), from trādō (“give up, hand over, deliver over, betray”, verb), from trāns- (“over, across”) + dō (“give”).
treason.g: The crime of betraying one’s own country.

treasure.e: From Middle English tresour, from Old French tresor (“treasury”), from Latin thēsaurus (“treasure”), from Ancient Greek θησαυρός (thēsaurós, “treasure house”). Mostly displaced native Old English goldhord (See goldhoard) and Old English ġestrēon.
treasure.g: A collection of valuable things; accumulated wealth; a stock of money, jewels, etc.

treasurer.e: From Middle English tresorer, from Old French tresorer, from tresor + -er.
treasurer.g: The government official in charge of the Treasury.

treasury.e: From Middle English tresorie, from Old French tresorie, from tresor (“treasure”), from Latin thēsaurus (“treasure”), from Ancient Greek θησαυρός (thēsaurós, “treasure house”).
treasury.g: A place where treasure is stored safely.

treat.e: From Middle English treten, from Anglo-Norman treter, Old French tretier, traiter, from Latin tractāre (“to pull", "to manage”), from the past participle stem of trahere (“to draw", "to pull”).
treat.g: To negotiate, discuss terms, bargain (for or with).

treatise.e: From Middle English tretys, from Anglo-Norman tretiz and Old French traitis (“treatise, account”), from traitier (“to deal with, treat”).
treatise.g: A formal, usually lengthy, systematic discourse on some subject.

treatment.g: The process or manner of treating someone or something.

tree.e: From Middle English trau, tre, tree, treo, treou, trew, trewe, troe, trouȝh, trouȝgh, trow, trowe, from Old English trēo, trēow, trēu, trīo, trīow, trȳw (“tree; wood; forest; beam, cudgel, log; cross”), from Proto-West Germanic *treu, from Proto-Germanic *trewą (“tree”).
tree.g: A perennial woody plant taller and larger than a shrub with a wooden trunk and, at some distance from the ground, having leaves and branches

tremble.e: From Middle English tremblen, from Old French trembler, from Late Latin tremulāre, ultimately from Latin tremere (“quiver, shake”).

tremendous.e: Adapted borrowing of Latin tremendus (“fearful, terrible”, gerundive of tremō (“to tremble”)) + -ous.

trench.e: Borrowed into Middle English from Old French trenche. Possible doublet of English: truncate.
trench.g: A long, narrow ditch or hole in the ground; either manmade, or formed naturally through erosion or tectonic plate movement.

trespass.e: Borrowed into Middle English trespas, from Old French trespas (“passage; offense against the law”), from trespasser.
trespass.g: An intentional interference with another's property or person.

trespass.e: From Middle English trespassen, borrowed from Old French trespasser (“to go across or over, transgress”), from tres- (“across, over”) + passer (“to pass”).
trespass.g: To commit an offence; to sin.

tress.e: From Middle English tresse, from Old French tresce, of uncertain origin; possibly from Vulgar Latin *trichia, from Ancient Greek τριχία (trikhía, “rope”), from θρίξ (thríx, “hair”).
tress.g: A braid, knot, or curl, of hair; a ringlet.

trial.e: From Middle English trial, triall, from Anglo-Norman trial, triel, from trier (“to pick out, cull”) + -al.
trial.g: An occasion on which a person or thing is tested to find out how well they perform or how suitable they are.

trial.e: From Latin tri- (stem of trēs (“three”)) + -al, on the pattern of dual.
trial.g: Characterized by having three (usually equivalent) components.

tribal.e: From Latin tribālis. By surface analysis, tribe + -al, first attested in the 1630s. The specific adjectival sense under the defunct theory of recapitulation derives from tribal history as an overly literal learned borrowing from German Stammesgeschichte; ordinarily, Stamm would only be translated as tribe when used in its ethnographic sense.

tribe.e: From Middle English tribe, tribu, from Old French tribu, from Latin tribus.
tribe.g: An ethnic group larger than a band or clan (and which may contain clans) but smaller than a nation (and which in turn may constitute a natio

tribulation.e: From Middle English tribulation, from Old French tribulacion, from Late Latin trībulātiō (“distress, trouble, tribulation, affliction”), from Latin tribulāre (“to press, probably also thresh out grain”), from trībulum (“a sledge consisting of a wooden block studded with sharp pieces of flint or with iron teeth, used for threshing grain”).
tribulation.g: Any adversity; a trying period or event.

tributary.e: From Middle English tributarie (“paying tribute”), from Latin tribūtārius, from tribūtum (“tribute”).
tributary.g: A natural water stream that flows into a larger river or other body of water.

tribute.e: From Middle English tribut (14th c.), from Middle French tribut, from Latin tributum (“tribute”, literally “a thing contributed or paid”), past participle of tribuere (“to assign, allot”), usually derived from tribus (whence English tribe).
tribute.g: An acknowledgment of gratitude, respect or admiration; an accompanying gift.

trickle.e: From Middle English triklen, likely a rebracketing (e.g. teres strikled > teerys trikled (“tears trickled”)) of Middle English striklen (“to trickle”), equivalent to strike + -le. For other similar cases of incorrect division, see also apron, daffodil, newt, nickname, orange, umpire.

trie.g: An ordered tree data structure that is used to store an associative array where the keys are usually strings.

tried.e: From Middle English tried, tryed, equivalent to try + -ed.
tried.g: Tested, hence, proven to be firm or reliable.

trim.e: From Middle English trimen, trymen, trümen, from Old English trymman (“to make firm; strengthen”), from Proto-West Germanic *trummjan, from Proto-Germanic *trumjaną (“to make fast; strengthen”), from Proto-Germanic *trumaz (“firm; strong; sound”).
trim.g: To reduce slightly; to cut; especially, to remove excess.

trimmer.e: From trim + -er. Figurative sense of “person who changes views with prevailing opinions” from 1680s, from nautical sense of “adjust sails with the wind”.
trimmer.g: One who trims, arranges, fits, or ornaments.

trip.e: From Middle English trippen (“tread or step lightly and nimbly, skip, dance”), perhaps from Old French triper (“to hop or dance around, strike with the feet”), from a Frankish source; or alternatively from Middle Dutch trippen (“to skip, trip, hop, stamp, trample”) (> Modern Dutch trippelen (“to toddle, patter, trip”)). Related also to trap, tramp.
trip.g: A journey; an excursion or jaunt.

trip.e: From Middle English tryppe, from Old French trippe. Possibly related to troop.
trip.g: A herd or flock of sheep, goats, etc.

triumph.e: From Middle English, borrowed from Old French triumphe, from Latin triumphus (“triumphal procession”), ultimately from Ancient Greek θρίαμβος (thríambos, “thriambus”).
triumph.g: A conclusive success following an effort, conflict, or confrontation of obstacles; victory; conquest.
To celebrate victory with pomp; to rejoice over success; to exult in an advantage gained; to exhibit exultation.

triumphant.e: From Old French, from Latin triumphāns, present participle of triumphō (“to triumph; to exult, rejoice”). By surface analysis, triumph + -ant (adjectival suffix).

trivial.e: From Latin triviālis (“appropriate to the street-corner, commonplace, vulgar”), from trivium (“place where three roads meet”). From the distinction between trivium (“the lower division of the liberal arts.
trivial.g: Ignorable; of little significance or value.

trod.e: From Middle English trod, past participle of treden; see tread.
trod.g: To walk heavily or laboriously; plod; tread

trod.e: From Old English trodu (“track, trace”), from the same source as tread.

trouble.e: Verb is from Middle English troublen, trouble, borrowed from Old French troubler, trobler, trubler, metathetic variants of tourbler, torbler, turbler, from Vulgar Latin *turbulō, from Latin turbula (“disorderly group, a little crowd or people”), diminutive of turba (“stir; crowd”).

troubler.g: One who, or that which, troubles; a disturber.

troublous.e: From Middle English troublous, from Anglo-Norman troublous and Middle French troubleus, corresponding to trouble + -ous.
troublous.g: Of a liquid: thick, muddy, full of sediment.

trough.e: From Middle English trogh, from Old English troh, trog (“a trough, tub, basin, vessel for containing liquids or other materials”), from Proto-West Germanic *trog, from Proto-Germanic *trugą, *trugaz, from Proto-Indo-European *drukós, enlargement of *dóru (“tree”).
trough.g: A long, narrow container, open on top, for feeding or watering animals.

trousers.e: The unexplained intrusive second -r- is perhaps due to the influence of drawers. Old Irish tribus is probably a borrowing of Anglo-Norman tribuz, trebuz, from Old French trebus, from Old Occitan trebucs, trabucs, from Late Latin trabrugi, tribuces, tubruci (“leg-coverings”).
trousers.g: An article of clothing that covers the part of the body between the waist and the ankles or knees, and is divided into a separate part for e

trow.e: From Middle English trowen, trouwen, treuwen, treowen, trouen, from Old English trēowan, trīewan (“to trust”) and Old English trūwian (“to trust, confide”), from Proto-Germanic *trewwāną (“to trust”) and Proto-Germanic *trūwāną (“to trust”); both from Proto-Indo-European *drew- (“faithful, true”).

From Shetlandic and Orcadian Scots trow, from Norn *drou, *drau (compare 18th c. Norwegian drau, modern drov, drauv), from Old Norse draugr (“malevolent revenant”); along the variation drow, intermixed with Norn troll, from Old Norse trǫll (“troll, malevolent supernatural being”), a partial synonym to draugr.

trucebreaker.g: One who violates a truce, covenant, or engagement.

trudge.e: Mid-16th century. Original meaning was somewhat idiomatic, meaning "to walk using snowshoes." Probably of Scandinavian origin, compare Icelandic þrúga (“snowshoe”), Norwegian truga (“snowshoe”) and dialectal Swedish trudja (“snowshoe”).
trudge.g: A tramp, i.e. a long and tiring walk.

true.e: From Middle English treowe, trew, trewe, triwe, true, trwe, from Old English trēowe, trīewe (“faithful, true”), from Proto-Germanic *triwwiz (“faithful, true”), from pre-Germanic *drewh₂yos, from Proto-Indo-European *drewH- (“firm, hard, true”). For the semantic development, compare Latin robustus (“tough”) from robur (“red oak”).
true.g: Conforming to the actual state of reality or fact; factually correct.

truly.e: From Middle English truely, treuly, treuli, trewely, treoweliche, treowliche, from Old English trēowlīċe (“faithfully; truly”), equivalent to true + -ly.
truly.g: In accordance with the facts; truthfully, accurately.

trump.e: Possibly from French triomphe (“triumph”) or Old French triumphe. If so, it is a doublet of triumph and thriambus.
trump.g: The suit, in a game of cards, that outranks all others.

trump.e: From Middle English trumpe, trompe (“trumpet”), from Old French trompe (“horn, trump, trumpet”), from Frankish *trumpa (“trumpet”), from a common Germanic word of imitative origin.

trumpet.e: From Middle English trumpet, trumpette, trompette (“trumpet”), from Old French trompette (“trumpet”), diminutive of trompe (“horn, trump, trumpet”), from Frankish *trumpa, *trumba (“trumpet”), ultimately imitative.
trumpet.g: A musical instrument of the brass family, generally tuned to the key of B-flat; by extension, any type of lip-vibrated aerophone, most often

trumpeter.e: From trumpet + -er (occupational suffix) or + -er (agent noun suffix).

trunk.e: From Middle English tronke, trunke, from Old French tronc (“alms box, tree trunk, headless body”), from Latin truncus (“a stock, lopped tree trunk”), from truncus (“cut off, maimed, mutilated”). For the verb, compare French tronquer, and see truncate.

trust.e: From Middle English trust, trost (“trust, protection”). Long considered a borrowing from Old Norse traust (“confidence, help, protection”), from Proto-Germanic *traustą, but the root vocalism is incompatible, so trust has come to be considered a reflex of an unattested Old English *trust.
trust.g: Confidence in or reliance on some person or quality.

trustee.g: A person to whom property is legally committed in trust, to be applied either for the benefit of specified individuals (beneficiaries), or f

trusting.e: From Middle English trustyng, trostinge, tristynge, equivalent to trust + -ing.
trusting.g: Inclined to believe the claims or statements of others; inclined to confide readily; trustful.

trusty.e: From Middle English trusty, tristy, tresty, equivalent to trust + -y.

truth.e: From Middle English trouthe, from Old English trēowþ, from Proto-Germanic *triwwiþō, from *triwwiz + *-iþō. By surface analysis, true + -th.
truth.g: True facts, genuine depiction or statements of reality.

truthful.e: From truth + -ful. Piecewise doublet of trothful, from Middle English trouþeful.
truthful.g: Honest, and always telling the truth.

try.e: From Middle English trien (“to separate out, sift, choose, select, evaluate, try a legal case”), from Anglo-Norman trier, triher, triere (“to divide, separate, choose, select, prove, determine, try a case”), Old French trier (“to choose, pick out or separate from others, sift, cull”), of uncertain origin.
try.g: To attempt; to endeavour. Followed by infinitive.

try.e: From Middle English trye, trie, probably from Old French trié, past participle of Old French trier (“to try”).
